MANDATORY SINGLE-MODEL EXPERIMENT: train one independent model per category.
Do not implement ensembles, bagging, boosting of independent predictors, stacking,
multi-seed/checkpoint averaging, score/rank voting, mixtures of independently fitted
experts, or neural scores combined with separately fitted transition/popularity scores.
Each category must load exactly one independently trained model/checkpoint at prediction.
Jointly trained internal layers/features of one network are allowed. Four category
models are necessary for routing and do not constitute an ensemble. All hypotheses,
code generation, debugging, reviews and memory use must respect this constraint even
if an upstream generic prompt suggests an ensemble. The host audits the actual
predictor before accepting validation scores; violations fail the trial and consume
their training budget. Do not read other trials or reuse their trained checkpoints.

 ## Search results
The 2024–2026 search found related text–interaction alignment work, but no verified exact match combining GRU4Rec, a text encoder trained from scratch, and joint contrastive training. CLA-Rec (ICDM 2024) aligns LLM-derived description embeddings with collaborative representations, then uses a Transformer sequence encoder. CALRec (RecSys 2024) combines recommendation and contrastive objectives around pretrained PaLM-2. CTT (KDD 2025) uses BERT-base text embeddings and a Transformer. These support investigating semantic alignment, but their pretrained encoders and backbones do not satisfy this experiment’s constraints. Sources: [CLA-Rec](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/10884256/), [CALRec](https://research.google/pubs/calrec-contrastive-alignment-of-generative-llms-for-sequential-recommendation/), [CTT](https://csse.szu.edu.cn/attachment/cglr/1756969546_Conference-25-KDD-CTT.pdf).

A constraint-compatible hypothesis—not an established result from these papers—is one GRU4Rec network with randomly initialized token embeddings, mean-pooled title/description tokens, and a small projection jointly trained with item-ID embeddings. Fuse text and ID representations inside the network; optimize next-item prediction plus a lightly weighted item-ID/text contrastive loss. Use only observed training text, mask missing descriptions, and exclude repeated item IDs from contrastive negatives. This preserves one jointly trained predictor per category without external weights or separate scoring models. Older [EC4SRec](https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.01347) reports contrastive-learning benefits with GRU4Rec, supporting backbone compatibility, but does not establish that scratch-trained text features will improve this benchmark.

---

The closest architectural precedent is [MTAM (2020)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.08598): temporal gates modify recurrent state transitions and information filtering, with a time-aware GRU capturing short-term intent. Recent work supports distinguishing elapsed time from sequence order: [E-NSDE (NeurIPS 2024)](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2024/hash/7cdbd53dfbcf9a5263227555aac5b9cd-Abstract-Conference.html) models continuously evolving preferences and interval-dependent uncertainty, although its differential-equation backbone is outside the required GRU family. [FAAM-SR (2026)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ins.2026.123580) introduces a frequency-adaptive GRU balancing repetitive and exploratory behavior; relevant evidence for adaptive gating, but not specifically timestamp-driven forgetting.

A compatible experimental hypothesis—not an established result from these papers—is one jointly trained GRU whose reset/update gates receive log-transformed observed inter-event gaps. Alternatively, learn a bounded retention vector that attenuates the previous hidden state before the GRU update, allowing selective forgetting after long gaps. Compare ordinary GRU, gap-conditioned gates, and soft state attenuation under the fixed validation protocol. Use only timestamps already observed in each prefix; never require the unknown next interaction time. Skip padding updates and read the final nonpadding position of left-padded histories. Keep a single trained network and checkpoint per category; these sources do not establish that hard resets or temporal gating improve this particular Amazon benchmark.

---

GRU4Rec’s strongest directly relevant evidence favors BPR-max or cross-entropy over ordinary BPR/TOP1. BPR-max emphasizes high-scoring sampled negatives through softmax weights: −log Σⱼ softmax(r)ⱼ·sigmoid(r₊−rⱼ), plus weighted negative-score regularization. This avoids diluting gradients across many easy negatives. The official implementation also supports logQ sampling correction for cross-entropy, making sampling distribution and correction important experimental choices. [Original paper](https://hidasi.eu/assets/pdf/gru4rec_v2_cikm18.pdf), [official implementation](https://github.com/hidasib/GRU4Rec).

Recent evidence cautions against assuming harder negatives improve every category or tail. A 2024 sequential-recommendation study compared random, popularity, in-batch, mixed and adaptive sampling across three datasets with 20 repeats: uniform sampling favored popular items; popularity-based negatives sometimes balanced popularity bands while reducing aggregate accuracy. False negatives are another concern: unobserved items can represent genuine interests, as documented by UFNRec. Its teacher-based remedy should not be imported into this single-model experiment. [2024 sampling study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.17276), [UFNRec](https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.04116).

Practical hypothesis: compare BPR-max against sampled softmax using the same GRU4Rec backbone and candidate budgets; separately vary uniform versus mildly popularity-weighted sampling and a limited hard-negative fraction. Exclude padding, the positive target and observed training-history items; this cannot eliminate unknown false negatives. These are proposed ablations, not established Electronics gains.
